senses: to have no more, to be deprived of
la:verb:perdo.html:
per-do, dĭdi, ditum, 3 (old form of the
pres. subj. perduim, : perduis,; : perduit,; ; but esp. freq., perduint,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; .—As the pass. of perdo, only pereo, perditus, perire appear to be in good use.—The only classical example of a pass. form in the pres. is: perditur haec inter misero lux non sine votis, (K. and H. ad loc.), where Lachm., perh. needlessly, reads lux porgitur, the day seems too long for me.—In the pass. perdi, in late Lat.; v.infra), v. a., to make away with; to destroy, ruin; to squander, dissipate, throw away, waste, lose, etc. (class.; syn.: dissipo, perimo, deleo).
Lit.: aliquem perditum ire,: Juppiter fruges perdidit,: funditus civitatem,: se ipsum penitus,: perdere et affligere cives,: perdere et pessundare aliquem,: aliquem capitis,i. e. to charge with a capital offence,; : sumat, consumat, perdat,squander,; so, perde et peri,: perdere et profundere,to waste,: perdere tempus,: operam,; cf.: oleum et operam,: Decius amisit vitam: at non perdidit,: cur perdis adulescentem nobis? cur amat? Cur potat?.—In execrations (very common): di (deaeque omnes) te perduint, may the gods destroy you! See the passages with perduint cited init.—Pass. (late Lat.): verbis perderis ipse tuis, Prosp. Epigr.: impii de terrā perdentur,: quasi sterquilinium in fine perdetur, id. Job, 20, 7.—
Transf., in gen., to lose utterly or irrecoverably: eos (liberos),: omnes fructus industriae et fortunae,: litem,to lose one's cause,: libertatem,: dextram manum,: memoriam,: causam,: spem,: vitam,: perii hercle! nomen perdidi,i. e. I have quite forgotten the name,.—Pass. (late Lat.): si principis vita perditur,; (v. supra).—Of loss at play: ne perdiderit, non cessat perdere lusor,; .—Hence, perdĭtus, a, um, P. a., lost, i. e.,
Hopeless, desperate, ruined, past recovery (class.; syn. profligatus): perditus sum, i. q. perii,I am lost!; : per fortunas vide, ne puerum perditum perdamus,: perditus aere alieno,: lacrimis ac maerore perditus,: tu omnium mortalium perditissime,: rebus omnibus perditis,: senatoria judicia,: valetudo,.—
In partic., desperately in love; lost, ruined by love (poet.): amore haec perdita est,: in puellā,: amor,.—
Lost in a moral sense, abandoned, corrupt, profligate, flagitious, incorrigible: adulescens perditus ac dissolutus,: homo contaminatus, perditus, flagitiosus,: abjecti homines et perditi,; : homo perditā nequitiā,: perdita atque dissoluta consilia,: luxuriae ac lasciviae perditae,: nihil fieri potest miserius, nihil perditius, nihil foedius,; ; .—Hence, sup.: omnium mortalium perditissimus,; .—Adv.: perdĭtē.
In an abandoned manner, incorrigibly: se gerere,, A, 2.—
Desperately, excessively: amare,: conari,.

la:verb:perduco.gloss: to lead, conduct, convey, carry, guide or bring through or to a place; deliver
senses: to lead, conduct, convey, carry, guide or bring through or to a place; deliver
to spread over, bedaub, coat, besmear
to rub out, erase, cross through
to take a drink, drink off or up, quaff, drain
to bring, carry or guide someone or something to a certain condition
to draw out, lengthen, prolong, continue; spend, pass
to draw or bring over, win over, persuade, induce (+ in/ad + Accusative case)
la:verb:perduco.html:
per-dūco, xi, ctum, 3 (
imper. perduce for perduc, ), v. a., lit., to lead or bring through; hence,
To lead, bring, conduct, guide a person or thing to any place.
In gen. (class.): filium illuc,: legiones ad aliquem,: comprehensos eos ad Caesarem perduxerunt,; cf. : legionem in Allobrogas,: Cyrum ad angustias,: nautas ad aequora,: ad Sullam,: in theatrum,: aliquem in conspectum alicujus,: bovem errantem ad stabula,: tauros ad sacrificium,.—
In partic.
To draw over, bring over a woman to the acceptance of a lover: huc Tertia perducta est,; ; ; ; ; ; .—
To bring, carry, lead, conduct to a place; of buildings, ditches, water (esp. freq. in Front.): a lacu Lemano ad montem Juram murum perducit,: munitiones ex castellis,: porticum,: longum opus,: Appia (aqua) perducta est,; cf.: tum duumviri aquae perducendae creati sunt,; and: aquas in urbem perducere,; so, Anionem in Capitolium,: virginem in agro Lucullano collectam Romam,; 13 et saep.: navigabilem alveum ex portu in Nilum,.—
Of money, to deliver: pecuniam,.—
Transf.
To spread over, bedaub, besmear with any thing (poet.): corpus odore ambrosiae,; : corpus stercore gallinae,: artus succo,: crusta perducta,.—
To rub out, erase (post-class.): si aliquid interleverit, perduxerit,: nomen in testamento,; .—
To take a drink, to drink off or up, to quaff (post-class.): cyceonis liquorem, Arn. poët. 5, 175: poculum continuo haustu,: aloë ex aquae cyathis tribus frigidis perducta,—
Trop.
In gen., to draw out, lengthen, prolong, continue, to bring, carry, guide a person or thing to a certain goal, to a certain period, etc. (class.): res disputatione ad mediam noctem perducitur,: oppugnatio ad noctem perducta,: in noctem orationibus perductis,: ad tempus tuum,: se medicinā usque ad longam senectam,: aliquem ex humili loco ad summam dignitatem,; so, aliquem ad amplissimos honores,: (agri colendi studia) ad centesimum annum,: artem ad magnam gloriam,: aliquem ad perniciem,: aliquid ad effectum,: aliquid ad exitum,: aliquid ad finem,: eo rem perduxit,brought the matter to that pass,; cf. Planc. ap. : aliquid ad liquidum confessumque,.—
To pass, spend: noctes,.—
In partic., to draw or bring over, win over, to persuade, induce (to an opinion or an action, etc.; class.): si dictis nequis perduci, ut vera haec credas,: perducebam illam ad me suadelā meā,: aliquem ad suam sententiam,; for which: aliquem in suam sententiam,: aliquem ad se magnis pollicitationibus,to bring over to one's side, to gain over,: hominem ad HS LXXX.,to induce to pay,.

per-dŏmo, ŭi, ĭtum, āre, v. a.
To tame or subdue thoroughly, to subjugate completely, to conquer, vanquish, overcome, etc. (Aug.; syn. subigo): ad perdomandum Latium exercitum circumducere,: Hispaniam,: Apulia perdomita,: gentes,: regionem,: urbes,: serpentes, tauros feroces,to tame, subdue,; : boves,.—
Transf., to work thoroughly, to knead: farinam assiduā tractatione,; cf.: perdomitam saxo Cererem, prepared, i. e. ground, .—
Trop.: ut nono demum sulco (solum) perdometur,.

la:noun:perduellio.html:
perdŭellĭo, ōnis, f.
perduellis
.
Hostile conduct against one's country, treason, whether consisting of an attempt against the state, its institutions, and chief ruler, or of union with a foreign enemy, desertion, etc. (class.): qui perduellionis reus est, hostili animo adversus rempublicam vel principem animatus est,; : (Clodius) actionem perduellionis intenderat (for causing the execution of the Catilinarians who were Roman citizens),: perduellionis judicium,: tum Sempronius, perduellionis se judicare Cn. Fulvio dixit, that he accused Fulvius of high-treason (for allowing himself to be defeated), : duumviros, qui Horatio perduellionem judicent, secundum legem facio (for killing his sister, which was regarded as a usurpation of the prerogative of punishment, and hence as a crime against the state),: diem perduellionis alicui dicere,; cf. ; .—*
Transf., concr., a (foreign) enemy of one's country, a public enemy; for the usual hostis (censured as a bombastic expression), ; cf. .

la:noun:perduellis.html:
per-dŭellis, is (
gen. plur. perduellūm, Att. ap. , or Trag. Rel. p. 238 Rib.; abl. perdvellibus, Enn. ap. Müll., or p. 146 Vahl.), m.
per-duellum, i. e. bellum
, a public enemy, an enemy actually waging war against a country (mostly anteclass. for the class. hostis): quos nos hostes appellamus, eos veteres perduelles appellabant, per eam adjectionem indicantes, cum quibus bellum esset,: equidem illud etiam animadverto, quod qui proprio nomine perduellis esset, is hostis vocaretur, lenitate verbi tristitiam rei mitigante,; Müll.: apud Ennium perduelles dicuntur hostes, ib.: perduelles superati, S. C. ap. : pirata non est ex perduellium numero, sed communis hostis omnium,; ; ; ; ; ; .—
Transf., a private enemy, an enemy, = inimicus (Plautin.), ; cf. .— Perduellis seems never to mean traitor to one's country (cf. perduellio); in this sense parricida is used instead.

la:verb:perdoceo.html:
per-dŏcĕo, cui, ctum, 2, v. a.,
to teach or instruct thoroughly (rare but class.; syn. erudio): res difficilis ad perdocendum,: aliquem,: quanti istuc unum me coquitare perdoces?: si quid Apollo Utile mortales perdocet ore meo,: homines,: suam stultitiam,to betray,.—With object-clause: dignam Maeoniis Phaeacida condere chartis Cum te Pierides perdocuere tuae,.—Hence, perdoctus, a, um, P. a., very learned, very skilful (rare but class.), ; : homo,: genitor,: exitio,.—Adv.: perdoctē, very skilfully (ante-class.), .
